senses.definition: Only possible if another thing happens first.
senses.simpleDefinition: Only possible if another thing happens first.
examples: The grant is contingent on final approval.
Our trip is contingent on the weather.
senses.synonymNote: Contingent on usually introduces a condition; dependent on can also describe a continuing need.

senses.definition: Not clear enough to show one definite meaning or opinion.
senses.simpleDefinition: Not clear enough to show one definite meaning or opinion.
examples: Her equivocal reply left both teams unsure.
The results were equivocal, so we ran another test.
senses.synonymNote: Equivocal often suggests two possible readings; unclear can simply mean hard to understand.

senses.definition: To make something harmful less serious.
senses.simpleDefinition: To make something harmful less serious.
examples: Trees can mitigate the heat in a crowded street.
The extra checks helped mitigate the risk.
senses.synonymNote: Mitigate usually concerns harm or risk; reduce can concern any amount.

senses.definition: To give further evidence that a statement is true.
senses.simpleDefinition: To give further evidence that a statement is true.
examples: The receipts corroborate her account of the journey.
Two witnesses corroborate the driver's description.
senses.synonymNote: Corroborate specifically means supporting a claim with evidence.

senses.definition: To provide evidence that shows a claim has a sound basis.
senses.simpleDefinition: To provide evidence that shows a claim has a sound basis.
examples: The company could not substantiate its promise.
We need data to substantiate the conclusion.
senses.synonymNote: Substantiate stresses providing a basis; corroborate adds evidence to an existing account.

senses.definition: To make something weaker or less trusted.
senses.simpleDefinition: To make something weaker or less trusted.
examples: Repeated delays undermine trust in the service.
The missing records undermine the report's conclusion.
senses.synonymNote: Undermine often describes a gradual or indirect weakening.

senses.definition: To make an existing problem worse.
senses.simpleDefinition: To make an existing problem worse.
examples: A lack of sleep can exacerbate stress.
The sudden closure may exacerbate traffic problems.
senses.synonymNote: Exacerbate normally takes a problem or harmful condition as its object.

senses.definition: To prevent something or make it impossible.
senses.simpleDefinition: To prevent something or make it impossible.
examples: The narrow doorway may preclude wheelchair access.
These findings do not preclude other explanations.
senses.synonymNote: Preclude often means that a condition rules out a possibility.

senses.definition: To take the place of something that was used before.
senses.simpleDefinition: To take the place of something that was used before.
examples: Digital tickets may supplant paper passes.
The new method did not supplant every older technique.
senses.synonymNote: Supplant suggests taking over an established role.

senses.definition: To add something useful that makes another thing work better.
senses.simpleDefinition: To add something useful that makes another thing work better.
examples: The diagrams complement the written guide.
Practical lessons complement the theory classes.
senses.synonymNote: Complement stresses a good fit; supplement stresses adding extra material.

senses.definition: To treat different things as if they were the same.
senses.simpleDefinition: To treat different things as if they were the same.
examples: Do not conflate low cost with good value.
The article appears to conflate income and wealth.
senses.synonymNote: Conflate specifically means combining distinct ideas or categories.

senses.definition: To find a way for apparently different ideas or needs to fit together.
senses.simpleDefinition: To find a way for apparently different ideas or needs to fit together.
examples: We must reconcile the two accounts of the event.
The plan tries to reconcile lower costs with better care.
senses.synonymNote: Reconcile often starts with a conflict; harmonise may simply mean bringing things into agreement.

senses.definition: To examine something very carefully.
senses.simpleDefinition: To examine something very carefully.
examples: Please scrutinise the figures before signing.
The panel will scrutinise every expense claim.
senses.synonymNote: Scrutinise implies close attention to detail, not just looking at something.

senses.definition: To make something easier to understand by explaining it.
senses.simpleDefinition: To make something easier to understand by explaining it.
examples: A simple diagram can elucidate the process.
The speaker used an example to elucidate the rule.
senses.synonymNote: Elucidate is formal and usually means explaining an idea in more detail.

senses.definition: To limit a statement so that it is more exact.
senses.simpleDefinition: To limit a statement so that it is more exact.
examples: I should qualify my earlier claim: the result applies only to adults.
The authors qualify their conclusion by noting the small sample.
senses.synonymNote: In this sense, qualify adds a condition or limit to a claim; it does not mean passing a test.

senses.definition: To admit that something is true, often after resisting it.
senses.simpleDefinition: To admit that something is true, often after resisting it.
examples: She had to concede that the old route was faster.
The manager will concede that the service needs work.
senses.synonymNote: Concede often involves accepting an unwelcome point in a disagreement.

senses.definition: To reach an idea from the information available.
senses.simpleDefinition: To reach an idea from the information available.
examples: We cannot infer a cause from this pattern alone.
Readers may infer that the narrator is worried.
senses.synonymNote: Infer is broad; deduce often suggests a more formal chain of reasoning.

senses.definition: To say that something is caused by a particular thing.
senses.simpleDefinition: To say that something is caused by a particular thing.
examples: The team cannot attribute the rise to one factor.
She chose to attribute the error to a misunderstanding.
senses.synonymNote: Attribute and ascribe both link a result to a cause; attribute is more common.

senses.definition: To notice or recognise something that is not obvious.
senses.simpleDefinition: To notice or recognise something that is not obvious.
examples: It was hard to discern a pattern in the data.
With practice, you can discern small differences in tone.
senses.synonymNote: Discern often involves understanding a difference, while detect can mean simply noticing a presence.

senses.definition: Not yet certain or finally agreed.
senses.simpleDefinition: Not yet certain or finally agreed.
examples: We made a tentative plan for Friday.
The report offers only a tentative explanation.
senses.synonymNote: Tentative stresses uncertainty; provisional stresses waiting for a final version.

senses.definition: Used for now but likely to be reviewed or changed.
senses.simpleDefinition: Used for now but likely to be reviewed or changed.
examples: The team announced a provisional timetable.
Her acceptance is provisional until the documents arrive.
senses.synonymNote: Provisional usually anticipates confirmation or revision; temporary only says something will not last.

senses.definition: Seeming reasonable or possibly true.
senses.simpleDefinition: Seeming reasonable or possibly true.
examples: That is a plausible explanation for the delay.
The story sounds plausible, but we need evidence.
senses.synonymNote: Plausible means a claim could be true; credible may imply stronger reasons to trust it.

senses.definition: Able to be defended with good reasons.
senses.simpleDefinition: Able to be defended with good reasons.
examples: That position is no longer tenable after the new evidence.
Is the assumption tenable in a small town?
senses.synonymNote: Tenable normally describes a claim or position that can withstand criticism.

senses.definition: Especially important or easy to notice in the situation.
senses.simpleDefinition: Especially important or easy to notice in the situation.
examples: The summary should include the salient points.
Cost was the most salient concern in the discussion.
senses.synonymNote: Salient stresses relevance or importance; prominent can simply mean highly visible.

senses.definition: Directly related to the matter being discussed.
senses.simpleDefinition: Directly related to the matter being discussed.
examples: Please raise questions that are germane to the proposal.
Her experience is germane to this debate.
senses.synonymNote: Germane is a formal way to say directly relevant to the current subject.

senses.definition: So different that they do not naturally form one group.
senses.simpleDefinition: So different that they do not naturally form one group.
examples: The project brings together disparate sources of data.
The committee must balance disparate interests.
senses.synonymNote: Disparate stresses a lack of similarity; diverse may simply mean varied.

senses.definition: Done by accident rather than on purpose.
senses.simpleDefinition: Done by accident rather than on purpose.
examples: The omission was inadvertent, and we corrected it.
An inadvertent click closed the form.
senses.synonymNote: Inadvertent often describes an action caused by a lack of attention.

senses.definition: So small that it has little practical effect.
senses.simpleDefinition: So small that it has little practical effect.
examples: The difference in travel time was negligible.
The change had a negligible effect on total costs.
senses.synonymNote: Negligible means too small to matter in context, not merely small in size.

senses.definition: Large enough in amount or importance to matter.
senses.simpleDefinition: Large enough in amount or importance to matter.
examples: The repair will require substantial funding.
The two versions contain substantial differences.
senses.synonymNote: Substantial often suggests practical importance as well as size.

senses.definition: Matching something in size, amount or degree.
senses.simpleDefinition: Matching something in size, amount or degree.
examples: Pay should be commensurate with responsibility.
The response was not commensurate with the scale of the problem.
senses.synonymNote: Commensurate with compares levels; proportionate to often judges whether a response is suitably sized.

senses.definition: Existing as a basic part of something.
senses.simpleDefinition: Existing as a basic part of something.
examples: There are risks inherent in any new project.
The method has an inherent limit: it cannot show cause.
senses.synonymNote: Both mean built into something; inherent often describes a quality or risk.

senses.definition: Found almost everywhere in a particular setting.
senses.simpleDefinition: Found almost everywhere in a particular setting.
examples: Mobile payment signs have become ubiquitous in the city.
The phrase is ubiquitous in business reports.
senses.synonymNote: Ubiquitous suggests almost everywhere; widespread only means many places.

senses.definition: Able to recover after difficulty or change.
senses.simpleDefinition: Able to recover after difficulty or change.
examples: A resilient system can keep working after one part fails.
The community proved resilient after the flood.
senses.synonymNote: Resilient stresses recovery; robust stresses strength or resistance to failure.

senses.definition: Very strict and carefully enforced.
senses.simpleDefinition: Very strict and carefully enforced.
examples: The laboratory follows stringent safety rules.
Applicants face stringent checks before approval.
senses.synonymNote: Stringent often describes demanding rules or standards.

senses.definition: Based on no clear reason, rule or fair method.
senses.simpleDefinition: Based on no clear reason, rule or fair method.
examples: The cut-off date seemed arbitrary.
We need consistent criteria rather than arbitrary choices.
senses.synonymNote: Arbitrary lacks a defensible reason; random may follow a deliberate chance-based method.

senses.definition: Having both positive and negative feelings about something.
senses.simpleDefinition: Having both positive and negative feelings about something.
examples: She felt ambivalent about leaving her job.
Residents remain ambivalent about the new development.
senses.synonymNote: Ambivalent means mixed feelings, not simply a lack of information.

senses.definition: Not favouring one side unfairly.
senses.simpleDefinition: Not favouring one side unfairly.
examples: An impartial reviewer should assess the complaint.
The chair must remain impartial during the vote.
senses.synonymNote: Both reject unfair preference; impartial often concerns fair treatment of opposing sides.

senses.definition: Focused on what can work in practice.
senses.simpleDefinition: Focused on what can work in practice.
examples: We need a pragmatic response to the shortage.
The team took a pragmatic approach and tested a smaller version.
senses.synonymNote: Pragmatic often suggests accepting workable compromises instead of insisting on an ideal.

senses.definition: Clear, well supported and likely to persuade.
senses.simpleDefinition: Clear, well supported and likely to persuade.
examples: She presented a cogent argument for the change.
The report gives a cogent explanation of the failure.
senses.synonymNote: Cogent especially describes reasoning that is clear and logically strong.

senses.definition: Stated or appearing to be the reason, though the real one may differ.
senses.simpleDefinition: Stated or appearing to be the reason, though the real one may differ.
examples: The ostensible purpose of the meeting was to discuss costs.
He visited for the ostensible reason of returning a book.
senses.synonymNote: Ostensible often raises doubt about whether the stated purpose is genuine.

paragraphs.text: In November 2026, the IEA reported that energy security was encouraging more countries to expand renewables. Yet adding generating equipment was not enough: electricity networks also needed investment. Projects awaiting connection illustrated this constraint.

The agency also highlighted storage and flexible demand. Moving some electricity use to periods of plentiful renewable supply could help systems use available generation more effectively. These measures support expansion; they do not make networks unnecessary.

At UNESCO's Digital Learning Week in September 2026, education representatives called for AI to support human judgement rather than replace it. They linked potential benefits to preparation and governance, not simply to access to a tool.

Their statement also stressed teacher participation in adoption decisions. This treats teachers as contributors to policy, not merely recipients of a finished product. The position permits carefully governed use without endorsing unrestricted adoption.

Fictional case study. A city tested later library opening hours at two branches for eight weeks. Evening visits rose by 18 per cent compared with the previous eight weeks. The period also included university examinations. The evaluation team therefore described the increase as encouraging but could not attribute it solely to the new hours.

Maya, the service manager, wanted to extend the trial before committing to permanent staffing costs. Arun, the finance officer, asked for the cost per additional visit and warned that high attendance alone would not establish value for money. Leila, a community organiser, requested a survey of people who had not attended; current visitors could not represent everyone who might need the service.

The next phase will add two comparison branches that retain their normal hours. Both groups will record visits using the same method. The team will publish the results after twelve weeks. A decision on permanent opening hours is contingent on that review; no permanent change has yet been approved.

passages.title: A repair service changes its rules

paragraphs.text: Fictional case study. A community workshop accepts small household devices for assessment. Customers first submit a description of the fault. A technician then inspects the item and provides a written estimate. Repairs begin only after the customer approves that estimate. If parts cannot be obtained, the workshop returns the item without carrying out a repair.

A proposed notice says, 'Every device will be fixed within seven days.' The coordinator rejects it because neither parts nor successful repair can be guaranteed. She instead proposes, 'We aim to assess each item within seven days and will contact you before any chargeable repair.' The deadline concerns assessment, not completion.

The service charges a five-pound assessment fee, payable even if repair is not possible. That fee is deducted from the final bill when a repair goes ahead. A volunteer suggests hiding the fee in small print to make the notice shorter. The coordinator objects: brevity should not obscure a condition that affects a customer's decision.

questions.explanation: She objects to hiding the fee: clear conditions matter more than brevity in that case.

questions.title: Agreement error
questions.instructions: Use the supplied text. Choose the best-supported answer.
questions.prompt: Select the erroneous segment: Each of the estimates / have been checked / by a second reviewer.
questions.explanation: Each is singular, so the verb should be has been checked. Of the estimates does not make the subject plural.

questions.title: Inversion error
questions.instructions: Use the supplied text. Choose the best-supported answer.
questions.prompt: Select the erroneous segment: Not until the audit ended / the committee released / its findings.
questions.explanation: After an initial negative time phrase, use inversion in the main clause: did the committee release.

questions.title: Paragraph precision
questions.instructions: Use the supplied text. Choose the best-supported answer.
questions.prompt: Replace this overstatement: 'Visits rose during the trial. Therefore, the longer hours caused the entire rise.'

options.text: Visits rose during the trial, but the available comparison does not isolate the effect of longer hours.
Visits rose, proving that every library needs longer hours.
Visits rose, so examinations had no effect.
Visits rose; therefore, the data are worthless.

questions.explanation: The first revision preserves the observed increase while limiting the causal claim. The other versions add unsupported conclusions.

questions.title: Paragraph order
questions.instructions: Complete the task using the supplied information.
questions.prompt: Arrange the sentences into a coherent paragraph.

items.text: The workshop received several complaints about unclear charges.
To investigate them, the coordinator reviewed the notice.
She found that the assessment fee appeared only in small print.
She therefore moved that condition beside the booking instructions.

questions.explanation: The complaints establish the problem, the review investigates it, the finding identifies the cause, and the final sentence gives the response.

questions.title: Condition cloze
questions.instructions: Use the supplied text. Choose the best-supported answer.
questions.prompt: The extension is contingent ___ an independent review.
questions.explanation: The fixed pattern is contingent on, meaning dependent on a condition.

questions.title: Open cloze
questions.instructions: Complete the task using the supplied information.
questions.prompt: Complete with ONE WORD: No sooner had the report appeared {{course:field-a}} questions arose about its methods.
questions.explanation: No sooner is paired with than. The first clause already contains the required inversion.

questions.title: Word formation
questions.instructions: Complete the task using the supplied information.
questions.prompt: Use RELY: The committee questioned the {{course:field-a}} of the figures.
questions.explanation: The noun reliability fits after the and before of. Reliable is an adjective and cannot fill this noun position.

questions.title: Key word change
questions.instructions: Complete the task using the supplied information.
questions.prompt: Use ACCOUNT without changing it. 'The panel ignored the cost.' Complete: The panel failed to {{course:field-a}}. Use FIVE WORDS.
questions.explanation: Take something into account means consider it. Failed to preserves the meaning that the cost was ignored.

questions.title: Dialogue evidence
questions.instructions: Use the supplied text. Choose the best-supported answer.
questions.prompt: A colleague asks, 'May I call this result conclusive?' The study has only ten participants. Choose the most careful reply.

options.text: Certainly; a small study proves every case.
I would qualify that claim until we have stronger evidence.
The claim is irrelevant because no small study has value.
No further evidence could ever help.

questions.explanation: Qualifying the claim acknowledges the limitation without dismissing the study or ruling out later evidence.

questions.title: Scenario notice
questions.instructions: Use the supplied text. Choose the best-supported answer.
questions.prompt: You must publish the workshop's service notice. Which wording is consistent with its rules?

options.text: Every item is repaired free within seven days.
Assessment normally precedes a written estimate; repair requires your approval.
Approval is assumed once an item arrives.
The assessment fee applies only to successful repairs.

questions.explanation: The second option preserves the process. The others invent guarantees, remove consent or misstate the fee.
